legend: The students at Rubgers University are organizing a programming contest. Since a lot of strong teams will participate, they expect some of them to solve all problems. To distinguish between them, a special prize will be awarded to the team with a special solve order.
The contest consists of N≤26$$$N \leq 26$$$ problems labelled A$$$\mathrm{A}$$$, B$$$\mathrm{B}$$$, etc: the first N$$$N$$$ letters of the English alphabet.

A solve order for a team is a sequence of letters denoting the order in which it solved all the problems: e.g., for N=3$$$N=3$$$, a possible solve order is BAC$$$\mathrm{BAC}$$$ — B$$$\mathrm{B}$$$ solved first, then A$$$\mathrm{A}$$$, then C$$$\mathrm{C}$$$. We only consider teams which solve every problem exactly once, so, e.g., AC$$$\mathrm{AC}$$$ or ABAC$$$\mathrm{ABAC}$$$ are not valid solve orders.

Solve order a$$$a$$$ is lexicographically smaller than solve order b$$$b$$$ if, at the first position where they differ, the character in a$$$a$$$ comes in the alphabet before the character in b$$$b$$$. E.g., ACB$$$\mathrm{ACB}$$$ is lexicographically smaller than BAC$$$\mathrm{BAC}$$$, which is lexicographically smaller than BCA$$$\mathrm{BCA}$$$.

Consider all possible solve orders of the N$$$N$$$ problems. Let their number be M$$$M$$$. Sort the M$$$M$$$ solve orders from lexicographically smallest to largest. In this list, the median solve order is located at position ⌈M2⌉$$$\lceil \frac{M}{2} \rceil$$$ (M2$$$\frac{M}{2}$$$ rounded up).
Any team with the median solve order will get a special prize. Help Rubgers students decide what the order is!
input: The problem consists of T$$$T$$$ independent test cases.
The first line contains a single integer T$$$T$$$ (1≤T≤26$$$1 \leq T \leq 26$$$) — the number of independent test cases to process.
Each of the next T$$$T$$$ lines contains a single integer N$$$N$$$ (1≤N≤26$$$1 \leq N \leq 26$$$) — the number of problems in the contest.
output: For each test case, output a single line containing the median solve order for the contest with N$$$N$$$ problems.
note: In the first test case, N=1$$$N=1$$$, so the only solve order is A$$$\mathrm{A}$$$.
In the second test case, the solve orders in lexicographical order are AB,BA$$$\mathrm{AB}, \mathrm{BA}$$$. The median is AB$$$\mathrm{AB}$$$.

In the third test case, the solve orders in lexicographical order are ABC,ACB,BAC,BCA,CAB,CBA$$$\mathrm{ABC}, \mathrm{ACB}, \mathrm{BAC}, \mathrm{BCA}, \mathrm{CAB}, \mathrm{CBA}$$$. The median is BAC$$$\mathrm{BAC}$$$.
